concepts.name: The SSE event format and reconnection
Streaming tool-call progress to the UI

questions.prompt: A chat UI sends each user message with a normal HTTP POST and needs the answer streamed back token by token. Which transport fits best, and why?

choices.text: WebSockets, because server-sent events can't carry JSON
Server-sent events, because the stream only flows from server to client and SSE runs over plain HTTP
WebSockets, because server-sent events never reconnect after a dropped connection
Long polling, because streaming responses don't work through proxies

questions.explanation: SSE is one-way, from server to client, which is exactly a streamed answer. It is plain HTTP with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, and the browser's `EventSource` reconnects on its own. `data:` lines can carry any text, including JSON. WebSockets are for two-way sessions where the client also sends a stream of messages.

questions.prompt: Your app opens one `EventSource` per browser tab over HTTP/1.1. Users with many tabs open say the seventh tab's stream never starts. Why?

choices.text: `EventSource` allows only one connection per page, and later ones wait in a queue
The server's `retry` field is too low, so the new tab gives up before connecting
Browsers cap HTTP/1.1 at about 6 connections per domain; each SSE stream holds one
SSE streams time out after six minutes, and the seventh tab starts too late

questions.explanation: MDN warns that without HTTP/2, SSE hits the browser's limit of 6 open connections per browser and domain, shared across all tabs, and browsers have marked this 'won't fix'. Over HTTP/2 the default is about 100 concurrent streams. Serve over HTTP/2, or share one stream between tabs.

questions.prompt: Compare server-sent events and WebSockets for streaming an agent's answer to a browser. When would you choose WebSockets instead?

model_answer.summary: SSE is a one-way stream over ordinary HTTP with built-in reconnection, which fits streamed answers. WebSockets are a two-way channel, worth it when the client must also send a continuous stream of messages.
key_points: SSE: one-way (server to client) over plain HTTP with `text/event-stream`, so it works with ordinary HTTP servers and proxies
SSE: the browser's `EventSource` reconnects automatically and sends `Last-Event-ID`, so the server can resume
`EventSource` only makes GET requests and only takes a `withCredentials` option, so no custom headers or body; a `fetch`-based reader can stream a POST response instead
WebSockets: a two-way interactive session, for cases like the user interrupting mid-stream, voice, or live collaboration
The classic `WebSocket` API has no backpressure: messages that arrive faster than you handle them get buffered

questions.explanation: Most chat UIs send a request and stream a response, so SSE (or a streamed HTTP response) is the simpler choice. Reach for WebSockets when the traffic really is two-way.

questions.prompt: Which bytes make one valid SSE message with the event name `tool` and a JSON payload?

choices.text: `event: tool`, then `data: {"name": "search"}`, then a blank line
`{"event": "tool", "data": {"name": "search"}}` on a single line
`type: tool`, then `data: {"name": "search"}`, then a blank line
`event: tool`, then `data: {"name": "search"}`, with no blank line until the stream closes

questions.explanation: An SSE message is a set of `field: value` lines ended by a blank line (two newlines). `event` sets the name, which the client handles with `addEventListener("tool", ...)`; `data` carries the payload. There is no `type` field, and without the blank line the browser doesn't dispatch the message yet.

questions.prompt: The connection drops halfway through a streamed answer and `EventSource` reconnects. How can the server continue without resending tokens the client already has?

choices.text: Put the number of tokens sent so far in the `retry` field of each event
Nothing is needed: `EventSource` buffers and replays the events it had already received
Send an HTTP 204 so the browser resumes the stream from where it stopped
Give each event an `id:`; on reconnect the browser sends it back as `Last-Event-ID`

questions.explanation: The `id` field sets the stream's last event ID, and the browser sends it as `Last-Event-ID` when it reconnects. The server can then skip what the client already has. `retry` only sets the reconnection delay in milliseconds, and an HTTP 204 response tells the browser to stop reconnecting.

questions.prompt: What does backpressure mean in a stream?

choices.text: The consumer signals up the chain so the producer slows down instead of filling a buffer
The server resends chunks the client didn't acknowledge, pushing them back into the stream
The client compresses chunks when the network is slow, to relieve the pressure on it
The producer sends chunks faster to empty its queue before the consumer falls behind

questions.explanation: MDN's Streams API describes backpressure as a stream later in the chain telling earlier ones to slow delivery when it isn't ready for more. Without it, a fast producer and a slow consumer mean an ever-growing buffer, and memory runs out. MDN notes that the classic `WebSocket` API has no backpressure for this reason.

questions.prompt: A proxy closes connections that are idle for 60 seconds. Your agent spends 90 seconds inside a tool call without sending any tokens, and the stream dies. What's the usual fix?

choices.text: Set the SSE `retry` field to 90000 so the proxy waits longer
Respond with HTTP 204 while the tool runs, then resume the stream
Send a comment line such as `: ping` every few seconds while idle
Raise the `EventSource` timeout option in the browser to 120 seconds

questions.explanation: Lines starting with `:` are SSE comments: the client ignores them, but they keep bytes flowing so proxies don't see the connection as idle. FastAPI's `EventSourceResponse` (FastAPI 0.135+) sends such a ping every 15 seconds on its own. `retry` only changes the reconnect delay, 204 ends the stream, and `EventSource` has no timeout option.

questions.prompt: A user closes the tab halfway through a long streamed answer. What should your server do?

choices.text: Nothing: the model provider stops generating as soon as the browser disconnects
Stop producing events and cancel the upstream model and tool calls, so you stop paying for tokens nobody will read
Keep streaming to the closed socket until the model finishes, so the answer is complete in the logs
Send HTTP 204 so the browser knows not to reconnect

questions.explanation: The provider only sees your server's connection to it, which stays open until your code closes it. Starlette notices the client's `http.disconnect` and stops the streaming response; your generator should then cancel the upstream request and clean up (in a `finally` block). An HTTP 204 is how a server tells a reconnecting client to stop; it can't reach a closed tab.

questions.prompt: Explain how a FastAPI SSE endpoint should handle a client that disconnects mid-stream, and why it matters for an LLM app.

model_answer.summary: Detect the disconnect, stop the stream, and cancel the work behind it, because an upstream model call keeps costing money until your server cancels it.
key_points: The server notices the disconnect (an ASGI `http.disconnect` message; Starlette stops the streaming response)
The generator stops producing, and cleanup runs in `finally`: cancel the upstream model request and any running tool calls
Otherwise the model keeps generating tokens that are billed but never read, and holds a connection and worker
Record the run as cancelled with the tokens used so far, rather than as an error or a success

questions.explanation: The browser's connection and your server's connection to the model are separate. Closing the first doesn't close the second: your code has to.

questions.prompt: Your agent should show "calling search..." while a tool runs, and keep streaming answer tokens on the same connection. Which design works best?

choices.text: Open a second SSE connection just for tool events, alongside the token stream
Insert the words "calling search..." into the text tokens so the client shows them
Poll a status endpoint once a second from the browser while the stream runs
Send typed events on one stream: token events for text, tool events for status

questions.explanation: One stream with typed events keeps everything in order and costs one connection. Named SSE events (`event: token`, `event: tool`) or typed JSON parts let the client render each kind differently; the AI SDK's UI message stream uses parts such as `text-delta`, `tool-input-available` and `tool-output-available`. Mixing status into the text pollutes the answer, and a second stream or polling loses ordering and adds connections.

questions.prompt: Design the events your server streams for one agent turn that calls one tool and then answers. What does each event carry?

model_answer.summary: Send typed events in order: tool started, tool finished, text deltas, then a finish or error event, with an ID that ties each tool's start and end together.
key_points: A tool-start event with the tool name and a tool-call ID, sent before the tool runs, so the UI can show "calling X..."
A tool-end event with the same ID and a status (success or error), and optionally a short result
Text-delta events carrying the answer tokens as they arrive
A final finish event (or an error event) so the client knows the turn is over

questions.explanation: The call ID is what lets the UI match a tool's start to its end when several tools run. The AI SDK's UI message stream protocol is a worked example: `tool-input-start`, `tool-input-available`, `tool-output-available`, `text-delta` and `finish` parts over SSE.
